profile.name: Cici Yang
profile.role: Digital Technologies and Computer Science teacher · Middlemore House tutor
introduction: I'm a Computer Science and Digital Technologies teacher at King's College, Auckland, teaching both Cambridge and NCEA.

I bring together a creative eye for design and strong programming skills. I enjoy both imagining what something could be and working out how to build it. That combination shapes my teaching: I want students to develop the creativity and technical confidence to turn their ideas into something real.
I joined King's in 2024, and this portfolio is a collection of my experiences, reflections and learning along the way.
philosophy: I came from a design background because I loved being creative. I didn't have a clear plan for where it would take me. I kept learning, trying things and following what interested me. Looking back, that has opened up opportunities I never expected.

That experience shapes how I see my students. I think young people are often capable of more than they realise. I hold high expectations, but I also want them to feel comfortable asking questions, making mistakes and having another go.

I learn from my students too. The way they approach a problem can make me rethink an explanation or try a different approach. I want my classroom to be a place where students feel they belong, are cared for and can do their best. I'm also continuing to learn how to include te reo Māori and Māori perspectives in ways that are relevant to what we're learning.
More than anything, I want my students to believe in themselves and discover what they are capable of.

growth.title: A new chapter at King's College
paragraphs: I joined King's College at the beginning of 2024, having previously taught at Marcellin College. The two schools were very different, and it took time to adjust. I was impressed by the resources available at King's, the strong academic focus and, most importantly, the College's commitment to developing well-rounded young people. This is a philosophy I really admire.

One of my biggest learning experiences was adapting to the Cambridge Computer Science curriculum, having previously been more familiar with NCEA. It challenged me to rethink aspects of my teaching and assessment.

growth.title: Finding my balance
paragraphs: As I became more familiar with Cambridge, I began to appreciate the strengths of both qualification pathways. Cambridge has helped me become more structured and deliberate in teaching theoretical knowledge and preparing students for examinations.

At the same time, I wanted to keep my NCEA Digital Technologies teaching creative and progressive. I continued looking for ways to give students more ownership of their learning through practical projects, emerging technologies and opportunities to create something of their own.

growth.title: Continuing to explore and grow
paragraphs: I have become increasingly interested in how emerging technologies, particularly AI, are changing what we teach and how students learn. The upcoming changes to the Digital Technologies and Computer Science curriculum have made me think more seriously about how we prepare students for the future.

Looking back over these three years, I feel I have grown in my understanding of different curriculum approaches. I am still learning how to find the right balance between academic rigour, creativity and student independence. That is something I want to keep working on.

evidence.title: From imagination to immersive worlds
evidence.summary: Using Delightex to help Year 9 students create interactive virtual worlds, explore coding and learn through testing and reflection.
evidence.need:
Year 9 is an opportunity to introduce students to Digital Technologies and hopefully spark an interest that stays with them.

I wanted students to experience technology in a different way. Rather than simply playing games or using VR, I wanted them to see that they could create their own virtual worlds, bring their ideas to life and make them interactive through coding.
evidence.practice:
I introduced students to Delightex, where they could design their own 3D environments and explore VR and AR.

I wanted to give them creative freedom, but also introduce computational thinking along the way. As students built their worlds, they explored coding concepts such as sequencing, events and conditional logic to make objects respond and interact.

An important part of the learning was asking students to step back and critique their own work. What worked well? What could be improved? How would someone else experience their virtual world?

I wanted them to understand that designing something is only the beginning. Testing, reflecting and improving are just as important.
evidence.reflection:
Coming from a design background, I really enjoy this kind of teaching. I love seeing students start with an idea and gradually turn it into something they can experience.

One thing I want to keep improving is the balance between creativity and coding. It's easy for students to spend all their time designing beautiful environments, so I need to make sure they also understand the computational thinking behind their interactive features.

Their excitement is a useful starting point, but I also need to hear students explain how sequencing, events and conditional logic make their interactions work. Those explanations would help me decide where further coding instruction is needed, alongside the creative design work.
evidence.next:
Next, I would like to make student reflection more visible by asking them to document what they changed, why they changed it and how their coding helped improve the experience.

My hope is that some of these students will leave Year 9 wanting to explore programming, game development or VR/AR further.
evidence.impact:
What I enjoyed most was seeing students become excited about what they could create.

VR and AR made the learning feel real. Instead of coding for the sake of coding, students had a reason to learn how programming works because they wanted to make something happen in their own worlds.

I also wanted them to move beyond being proud of a finished project and begin recognising where their design could be better. Being able to critique their own work is an important step towards becoming an independent creator.

evidence.title: Learning to think through a bug
evidence.summary: Helping students slow down, make sense of errors and build the confidence to work through a programming problem.
evidence.need:
I've noticed how quickly some students lose confidence when their code doesn't work. Some ask for help as soon as an error appears. Others keep changing things without understanding what went wrong.

I want them to see mistakes as a normal part of programming. Debugging takes patience: slowing down, looking carefully at what the code is doing and being willing to try again.
evidence.practice:
When a student asks me to fix their code, I try not to give them the answer straight away. I ask what they expected it to do, what actually happened and where they think the problem might be.

We read the error message, trace variables and test small sections of code. Sometimes talking it through with a classmate helps them spot something they missed.

I learn from these conversations too. A student's approach can show me where my explanation wasn't clear, or suggest another way to explain a concept. I'm still learning when to offer a prompt and when to step back and give them time.
evidence.reflection:
I've learnt that giving an answer too quickly can take away a useful learning opportunity. It's tempting to fix a small error and move on, but I want the student to understand why the change works.

I have high expectations because I believe students can grow. I also need to be patient and encouraging, and recognise that they won't all reach the same point at the same pace.

The students' comments about understanding their own code and practising debugging give me a useful perspective on this approach. I want to look at their explanations alongside successive code versions to see how independently they can explain a fix, especially when AI makes code easy to obtain.
evidence.next:
I want to make debugging a more deliberate part of our lessons, with students explaining their thinking, learning from one another and reflecting on how they solved a problem.

I also want them to use Python comments to record what they are trying, what they have tested and what has changed between versions. This would help make their thinking easier to follow.

I hope they take some of that confidence beyond programming: being willing to face something difficult, ask questions and keep trying.
evidence.impact:
The moments I value most are when a student says, “Oh, I see what I did wrong!” That moment of understanding matters to me.

I want students to become less worried about mistakes and more willing to investigate a problem themselves. Getting the code right on the first attempt isn't the only thing that matters. The thinking, testing and persistence are part of the learning too.

codeSample.title: A Python quiz in development
codeSample.description: This version 3 quiz example uses a list of dictionaries and comments to explain what the code is doing. It gives us something concrete to discuss when looking at testing, changes between versions and the thinking behind a program.
codeSample.code:
#This is my version 3 of my quiz, i m trialing out dictionary

score = 0

# Store all the quiz questions in a list
# Each question is stored as a dictionary
questions = [
    {
        "question": "1. Which function displays information on the screen?",
        "A": "A. input()",
        "B": "B. print()",
        "C": "C. display()",
        "D": "D. output()",
        "answer": "B"
    },
    {
        "question": "2. Which symbol is used to write a comment in Python?",
        "A": "A. //",
        "B": "B. /*",
        "C": "C. #",
        "D": "D. --",
        "answer": "C"
    },
    {
        "question": "3. Which data type stores whole numbers?",
        "A": "A. string",
        "B": "B. float",
        "C": "C. boolean",
        "D": "D. integer",
        "answer": "D"
    },
    {
        "question": "4. Which function allows the user to enter information?",
        "A": "A. input()",
        "B": "B. print()",
        "C": "C. enter()",
        "D": "D. answer()",
        "answer": "A"
    },
    {
        "question": "5. Which operator checks whether two values are equal?",
        "A": "A. =",
        "B": "B. ==",
        "C": "C. !=",
        "D": "D. >=",
        "answer": "B"
    }
]

# Go through each question in the questions list
for q in questions:

    # Display the question and its four possible answers
    print(q["question"])
    print(q["A"])
    print(q["B"])
    print(q["C"])
    print(q["D"])

    # Ask the player for an answer
    # .upper() changes lowercase answers such as "a" into "A"
    answer = input("Enter your answer (A/B/C/D): ").upper()

    # Check entered a valid option
    if answer not in ["A", "B", "C", "D"]:
        print("Error! Please enter A, B, C, or D.\n")

    # Check if answer matches the correct answer
    elif answer == q["answer"]:
        print("Correct!\n")
        score += 1

    # If it does not match, answer is incorrect
    else:
        print("Wrong! The correct answer was", q["answer"] + ".\n")

# final result
print("Quiz finished!")
print("Your score is", score, "out of", len(questions))

evidence.title: Rethinking Assessment in the Age of AI: From Final Products to Visible Learning
evidence.context: NCEA Levels 2 and 3 Digital Technologies · AI and assessment
evidence.summary: Reflecting on AI, authentic assessment and how I could make students’ development and independent understanding more visible in my NCEA programmes.
evidence.need:
Lauren's Term 4 professional learning presentation on AI and assessment has prompted me to think more deeply about how I design and assess digital technology projects.

One idea that particularly interested me was the distinction between two assessment approaches. Lane 1 involves controlled conditions where students demonstrate their knowledge independently. Lane 2 allows students to complete more open-ended tasks, using resources and tools outside the classroom, with clear expectations around AI use.

This is particularly relevant to Digital Technologies because my students already work in environments where independent research, software documentation, online tutorials and technical support are part of the development process.

In my NCEA Level 2 classes, students develop websites and programming outcomes. At Level 3, they work with Unity to design and build interactive and immersive experiences, including VR projects.

These are not tasks that can always be completed in one sitting. Students develop their outcomes over several weeks, solving problems, testing ideas, responding to feedback and refining their work.

I began asking myself whether our assessment practices fully reflect this process, especially now that AI-assisted coding and development tools are becoming increasingly accessible.

If students can use AI to generate code, suggest designs or produce documentation, how can I be confident that the evidence I assess genuinely demonstrates their own learning?

I do not think the answer is simply to prohibit AI or attempt to detect its use. I think we need to reconsider how students demonstrate knowledge, technical competence and independent decision-making throughout a project.
evidence.practice:
My recent experience with NCEA assessment and moderation has also made this reflection particularly relevant.

It has reminded me that an engaging or technically impressive student outcome does not automatically provide sufficient evidence for every requirement of an achievement standard.

Students may create something functional, but their documentation may not clearly demonstrate how they tested, refined or justified important technical decisions.

I have also reflected on how much time students spend preparing final assessment reports.

Sometimes the final report becomes a substantial task in itself, with students trying to reconstruct weeks of development through screenshots and written explanations.

I am beginning to question whether this is always the most effective way to capture learning.

It becomes even more complicated when generative AI can produce polished technical explanations that may not accurately represent what a student understands or has done.

Rather than relying primarily on a final report, I would like to explore ways of collecting evidence naturally throughout the development process.

My aim would not be to reduce the rigour of assessment, but to make the evidence more authentic, manageable and closely connected to students' actual work.
evidence.reflection:
Looking back, I think the most significant shift in my thinking is moving from asking whether students should be allowed to use AI to asking what evidence would genuinely demonstrate their own learning in an AI-supported environment.

I still value open-ended projects because they encourage creativity, independence and purposeful problem-solving. I do not want assessment conditions to remove these opportunities.

However, I also want to be confident that the grades I award are supported by authentic evidence of each student's knowledge, skills and decisions.

For my future curriculum planning, I would like to explore three connected improvements: clearer AI-use expectations, more visible development evidence and short opportunities for students to demonstrate their understanding independently.

I want to approach these changes carefully, learning from NZQA guidance, moderation feedback, student experience and discussion with colleagues.

My goal is not to make assessments impossible to complete with AI. It is to design learning and assessment experiences where students can use appropriate modern tools while still developing, demonstrating and taking ownership of the knowledge and skills that matter.

For me, that feels like an important direction for teaching Digital Technologies in the years ahead.
evidence.next:
I do not think it would be appropriate to redesign all my NCEA assessments at once.

I would prefer to begin with a small, carefully planned investigation.

One possibility would be to trial a revised assessment evidence process in a Level 2 programming project and a Level 3 Unity VR project.

I would begin by reviewing the relevant standards and existing assessment schedules, then identify where development checkpoints and an AI-use menu could be introduced without changing the achievement requirements.

During the projects, I could collect feedback about how clearly students understand the assessment expectations, whether the checkpoints help them reflect on their development and whether they find the evidence process manageable.

I would also want to evaluate my own workload.

Short individual conversations may improve visibility of student understanding, but they also take time. Any new assessment approach needs to be practical within our teaching environment.

At the end, I would compare the quality and completeness of assessment evidence, consider the outcomes of internal verification and moderation, and identify which changes are worth retaining.

I am particularly interested in whether a more continuous evidence-collection process might reduce the pressure of producing lengthy final reports while making students' learning more visible.

I recognise that this is a question to investigate rather than an outcome I can assume.

sections.title: What Lane 2 could mean for Digital Technologies
sections.text:
One thing I appreciate about Lauren's approach is that it begins with the learning outcome.

Before deciding whether AI should be permitted, we need to ask what students are actually being assessed on.

For example, when students are learning about a new programming concept, AI might be helpful for explaining unfamiliar terminology or suggesting approaches to a problem.

However, when a student is being assessed on their ability to implement a programming technique, the evidence must genuinely demonstrate their own achievement of that technique.

The distinction becomes important when I consider the NCEA standards I currently teach.

At Level 2, AS91893 focuses on digital media development, AS91896 on programming and AS91897 on development processes. At Level 3, AS91903, AS91906 and AS91907 extend these expectations to more complex digital outcomes, programming techniques and development practices.

Although students may work on one integrated project, the standards assess different knowledge and skills.

This has reminded me that AI permissions cannot necessarily be identical across an entire project.

A tool that is appropriate for researching design conventions may not be appropriate for generating the code being assessed under a programming standard. Similarly, AI may assist a student in understanding project-management techniques, but it cannot replace the student's own planning, trialling and decision-making evidence.

I would like to investigate how Lane 2 principles could be adapted to our existing NCEA assessment requirements while maintaining the authenticity of students' work.

sections.title: Making the development process more visible
sections.text:
One of the most useful ideas from Lauren's presentation was the concept of layered protection for open assessments.

The presentation emphasised meaningful tasks, accessible learning, visible development and verification.

I think this provides a useful framework for reconsidering how I support students.

For my NCEA programmes, I would like to introduce more structured checkpoints during project development.

At the beginning of a project, students could explain their intended outcome, identify user requirements and demonstrate their understanding of the technical skills they expect to use.

During development, they could maintain a record of important decisions, testing, debugging and changes. This might include dated code versions, annotated screenshots, short screen recordings or technical notes.

At selected checkpoints, I could ask students to demonstrate a feature they have implemented, explain how their code works or discuss why they chose one approach over another.

For example, a Level 2 programming student might explain how a function processes data, identify where validation occurs or demonstrate how they tested an invalid input.

A Level 3 Unity student might explain the interaction between a C# script and an XR component, identify a problem they encountered and demonstrate how they investigated it.

These short conversations would allow me to understand the student's thinking while the work is still developing.

I would also want to make the process supportive rather than intimidating. Not every student is equally confident explaining technical ideas verbally, so demonstrations, annotated code and written explanations should complement one another.

Importantly, these checkpoints would provide supporting evidence of authenticity and understanding. I would still need to ensure that the submitted work meets the specific criteria of each achievement standard.

sections.title: Rethinking my Level 2 programme
sections.text:
I can see several opportunities to apply this thinking to my Level 2 Digital Technologies curriculum.

For web development, I would like students to begin with an authentic brief that identifies a real user, purpose or problem.

Rather than simply completing a website and writing a report afterwards, students could document the development of the outcome as it happens.

This might include early wireframes, design alternatives, feedback from intended users, testing records and examples of how the interface changed.

I would be interested in allowing clearly defined AI support during appropriate learning stages, such as researching accessibility, comparing layout approaches or identifying possible usability issues.

However, I would want students to demonstrate their own application of the techniques required by the standards.

For programming, I would be more cautious about AI-generated code.

I want students to become confident using Python and understanding the logic behind the programs they create. If AI produces the solution without students developing the necessary knowledge, the assessment may no longer demonstrate their programming achievement.

I would like to explore a model where students can use approved tools to learn, investigate and ask questions, while completing and demonstrating the assessed programming work under conditions that establish their own contribution.

This could include shorter supervised programming tasks, incremental code reviews and individual explanations alongside the main project.

I think this would also help me identify misconceptions earlier and provide more targeted support before the assessment deadline.

sections.title: Rethinking my Level 3 Unity and VR programme
sections.text:
I see similar opportunities in my Level 3 programme, where students develop interactive experiences using Unity.

VR projects are particularly interesting because they combine several areas of learning: programming, three-dimensional design, user interaction, technical integration, testing and project management.

Students often need to investigate unfamiliar technical problems, work with documentation and experiment with different solutions.

I want to preserve this independence and creativity.

At the same time, the increasing capability of AI-assisted development tools raises questions about how students demonstrate their own skills.

For example, if a student uses AI to generate a C# script that controls an object in VR, a working demonstration alone would not necessarily establish that they understand or independently implemented the programming techniques required by AS91906.

I would therefore like to place more emphasis on students explaining and demonstrating important aspects of their own development.

This could include showing the progression of a script, discussing why a particular programming technique was selected, demonstrating testing with different inputs and explaining how an error was identified and corrected.

For AS91903, I would look for evidence of the student's own complex media techniques and decisions about user experience.

For AS91907, I would want the student to demonstrate genuine planning, trialling, stakeholder feedback and refinement.

My experience with the VR chemistry game developed for King's College Subject Selection Evening has reinforced the value of working towards authentic outcomes.

A real audience creates opportunities for meaningful usability feedback and encourages students to think beyond whether a project simply works.

I would like to build on this approach while making the technical and development evidence more visible throughout the assessment.

sections.title: Introducing an AI Menu for assessment
sections.text:
Another practical idea I took from Lauren's presentation was the use of an AI Menu.

Rather than telling students that AI is either completely allowed or completely prohibited, an assessment could explain which types of assistance are appropriate.

I would like to adapt this approach for Digital Technologies.

The menu could distinguish between AI used to explain concepts, summarise research, brainstorm ideas, plan development, suggest testing approaches, critique decisions, improve writing or generate code and media.

Each assessment would specify which activities are permitted, which require teacher guidance and which are not appropriate as evidence of the student's own achievement.

For example, using AI to understand what an error message means may be acceptable during an approved learning activity, while submitting AI-generated code as evidence of personally implementing an assessed programming technique would not be.

I would also like students to become more reflective about their use of AI.

Rather than simply declaring that ChatGPT was used, students could explain what assistance they received, what they checked and which decisions they made independently.

However, I recognise that an AI-use declaration alone does not establish authenticity. It needs to be supported by observed work and appropriate assessment evidence.

Any menu I develop would need to be reviewed against NZQA requirements, the relevant standards and King's College assessment policies before being used in formal assessment.

sections.title: Assessing understanding, not just polished outcomes
sections.text:
This reflection has made me think about the difference between producing an impressive outcome and developing genuine technical competence.

In Digital Technologies, students can sometimes become focused on making their project look finished.

They may spend considerable time improving visual details while paying less attention to the underlying programming, testing or reasoning.

AI-assisted tools could make this imbalance more pronounced because they can help produce sophisticated-looking results quickly.

I want students to feel proud of their finished outcomes, but I also want them to understand what they have created.

For me, a successful programming assessment should provide evidence that a student can explain their logic, understand their code, identify problems and make informed technical decisions.

Similarly, a successful digital media project should demonstrate purposeful design, appropriate techniques and a thoughtful response to user needs.

I would like to explore how assessment can give greater visibility to this thinking without creating an additional layer of unnecessary paperwork.

sections.title: Considering fairness and accessibility
sections.text:
I also recognise that changing assessment practices may introduce new challenges.

Not all students have equal access to paid AI tools, powerful computers or technical support outside school.

Some students may arrive with considerable programming experience, while others are still developing confidence in basic concepts.

I would not want an open assessment environment to create an unfair advantage for students who have access to more sophisticated tools.

Any Lane 2 approach would therefore need clear guidance, equitable access to approved resources and appropriate scaffolding.

I would also need to consider students who find oral explanations challenging or who need additional learning support.

A layered assessment approach should provide different ways for students to demonstrate their understanding while keeping the requirements of the standard consistent.

I think this is particularly important when assessing complex projects over an extended period.

sections.title: Privacy, authenticity and professional responsibility
sections.text:
Another area I need to understand more deeply is the responsible use of AI in assessment.

Students may not always recognise the risks of uploading personal information, confidential feedback or school documents into external AI systems.

I would want to make expectations clear and ensure that any tools used are approved and suitable for students.

I am also conscious that AI detectors are not a reliable basis for deciding whether a student completed their own work.

For this reason, I would prefer to focus on the evidence available through classroom observations, development records, technical demonstrations and conversations.

Where concerns arise, I would follow the College's assessment and authenticity procedures rather than making assumptions based on the apparent writing style of a report.

This is an area where I would value further guidance from NZQA, colleagues responsible for assessment and moderation, and the school's AI project team.

sections.title: My professional learning
sections.text:
Lauren's presentation has helped me see that AI in education is not only about teaching students how to use new tools.

It also challenges us to reconsider what we value in learning and how we recognise genuine achievement.

As a Digital Technologies teacher, I want students to understand and use contemporary development tools. At the same time, I believe they need strong foundations in programming, computational thinking, problem-solving and independent judgement.

I am beginning to see that assessment design has an important role in maintaining this balance.

I also recognise that I have more to learn about AI governance, assessment authenticity and how these ideas can be applied fairly and consistently within NCEA.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss these questions with Lauren, my department and colleagues responsible for assessment. I think there is value in sharing practical examples, including approaches that do not work as expected.

evidence.title: Learning from Cambridge AS Results
evidence.summary: Reviewing the 2025 YAN class results and planning earlier checks, targeted support and more independent explanation for the next cohort.
evidence.need: My 2025 Cambridge AS Computer Science class, 12.COM.ASb - YAN, had 11 students. These results have prompted me to reflect on the spread of achievement and how I can identify learning needs earlier with the next cohort.
evidence.practice:
Six of the 11 students received A grades (54.5%), two received B (18.2%), one D (9.1%), one E (9.1%) and one U (9.1%). Eight received A or B (72.7%), and ten received an A-E grade (90.9%). There were no C grades.

The mean is 73.4, while the median is 83. The scores range from 28 to 91, a spread of 63 points. The mean being below the median shows how the lower scores affect the average. These are summaries of the report's percentage column, not a claim about raw examination marks.

The six A grades are encouraging. At the same time, the D, E and U results remind me to look beyond the higher grades and consider how well my teaching supports students who are finding the course difficult. With 11 students, each result represents 9.1 percentage points, so percentages need to be read alongside the counts.
evidence.reflection:
I feel encouraged by the number of A grades in my class. I want to recognise that achievement while also thinking carefully about the students whose results were lower. A strong median can make the overall picture look reassuring, but it does not tell me whether every student had the foundations and support they needed.

I enjoy practical, creative work, and I want students to see what they can make with Computer Science. Cambridge AS also asks them to communicate their understanding independently. Looking at these results makes me want to be more deliberate about checking both: can a student work through a task with support, and can they explain or apply the idea later without that support?

I do not want my response to be simply to give more revision or more examination questions to everyone. I want to understand what each student needs, choose an appropriate response and check whether it helps. I also want to keep stretching students who are ready for more demanding work. My aim for the next cohort is to maintain ambition while identifying difficulties earlier and following up more consistently.

I want assessment to shape the next learning step: what needs to be recalled, explained again, practised with support or applied independently. The action plan below sets out what I intend to try with the next cohort and how I will check whether it helps.
evidence.next:
Before the 2027 course: establish a reliable starting point
Review any available component marks and comparable internal assessments. Use a short diagnostic at the start of the 2027 course covering prerequisite knowledge, code tracing, problem-solving and written explanation. Record the specific errors rather than relying only on a total score, and use them to plan initial support and extension.

Each week: revisit learning and hear from everyone
Build in short, low-stakes retrieval questions that revisit earlier topics. Ask every student to respond through an appropriate written or digital method, so my decisions are informed by more than the students who volunteer answers. If a misconception is common, revisit it with a different explanation; if it affects a few students, provide targeted practice. Check it again in a later lesson.

During each unit: model the thinking, then reduce support
Use worked examples to make the reasoning behind an explanation or solution visible. Move from a modelled example to guided practice and then an unfamiliar independent question. Include precise subject vocabulary and opportunities for students to explain why an answer or algorithm works. Use students' responses to judge when they are ready for less support.

At each checkpoint: target support and maintain challenge
For students whose work shows persistent difficulty, agree a small, specific learning goal and follow up within two to three weeks using a comparable task. Offer students who are secure more demanding applications and opportunities to justify alternative solutions. If progress is limited, change the support rather than repeating the same task and expecting a different result.

After each assessment: turn errors into the next teaching decision
Review responses by skill and, where available, examination component. Ask students to explain an error and improve their response before trying a related question independently. Keep brief records of recurring difficulties and the teaching response. Use timed practice to investigate examination performance after the underlying understanding has been checked.

At the end of each term: evaluate and adjust
Compare diagnostic, checkpoint and delayed-retrieval responses for the same learners. Look for more accurate explanations, fewer repeated misconceptions and successful independent application. At mock examinations, review component performance and the distribution of grades, not just the average. Use these findings to adjust teaching and support. When external results arrive, compare cohorts cautiously, taking account of class size and starting points rather than treating a percentage change as proof of teaching impact.
evidence.impact:
The results show a wide spread, but they do not tell me why it occurred. This report does not provide Paper 1 and Paper 2 marks, question-level performance, starting points, attendance or comparable mock results. I cannot identify a particular topic as a weakness or attribute a result to effort, confidence or a teaching strategy from this report alone.

My next step is to compare component results with students' earlier work and assessment responses. That would help distinguish gaps in knowledge from difficulties with application, explanation, programming or working under timed conditions. These are questions to investigate, not findings established by this report.

evidence.title: Beyond the Headset: Designing VR Experiences for a Real Audience
evidence.context: NCEA Level 3 Digital Technologies · VR development
evidence.summary: Designing a VR programme where technical skills and creative decisions come together in a chemistry game shared at Subject Selection Evening.
evidence.impact: A student's VR chemistry game became a working experience that could be demonstrated to students and parents at Subject Selection Evening.

sections.title: From a classroom project to a real experience
sections.text:
One of the things I enjoy most about teaching Digital Technologies is finding opportunities for students to create something that has a purpose beyond assessment.

When designing my NCEA Level 3 programme, I wanted students to explore virtual reality not simply as an exciting technology, but as a medium for solving problems, communicating ideas and creating meaningful experiences for others.

A particularly rewarding example was a student's VR chemistry game developed for King's College Subject Selection Evening, where students and parents could explore different subjects and discover what learning in Digital Technologies involves.

Seeing the student demonstrate the experience using a VR headset, with the gameplay displayed on a large screen, was a reminder of why I value authentic, project-based learning. What began as a classroom development project became an opportunity to showcase student creativity and technical capability to the wider College community.

sections.title: Designing the curriculum around creativity and technical challenge
sections.text:
Introducing VR development into the senior Digital Technologies curriculum required me to think carefully about how students would build the technical skills needed to realise their ideas.

I wanted the programme to move beyond following tutorials. Students needed opportunities to understand how an immersive environment works, experiment with interactions and make their own design decisions.

Using Unity and VR development tools, the learning involved exploring 3D environments, user interaction, scripting, testing and debugging.

I also wanted students to consider the user experience. A successful VR project is not just about making objects appear in a headset. The interactions need to be understandable, the environment needs to be purposeful, and the experience should communicate something meaningful to its intended audience.

The chemistry game demonstrated how a student could bring together technical development, creative design and knowledge from another subject to produce an engaging outcome.

sections.title: Sharing learning at Subject Selection Evening
sections.text:
What made this project particularly meaningful was the opportunity to share it with students and parents who were considering future subject choices.

Rather than simply explaining what Digital Technologies students learn, we could show them an example of what those skills can produce.

The VR chemistry game allowed visitors to see programming, interactive design and virtual reality working together in a student-created experience.

It also provided an opportunity to challenge the perception that Digital Technologies is only about learning to code. Programming was an essential part of the project, but so were creativity, design decisions, problem-solving and understanding how people interact with technology.

For me, this was an important reminder that authentic student work can be one of the most effective ways to communicate the value and possibilities of a subject.

sections.title: What this taught me about curriculum design
sections.text:
This experience reinforced my belief that senior Digital Technologies should give students the freedom to develop ambitious ideas while providing enough structure to support their technical learning.

VR development can be challenging. Students need to combine programming, spatial thinking, interaction design and problem-solving, often troubleshooting unexpected technical issues along the way.

As I continue refining the programme, I want to strengthen the progression from introductory technical exercises to independent project development. I would also like to provide more opportunities for students to test their work with people who have not been involved in creating it.

The experience has also encouraged me to consider further cross-curricular projects, where students could develop interactive experiences connected to Science, Geography, History or other learning areas.

sections.title: Looking ahead
sections.text:
What I found most rewarding was seeing a student use their technical skills to create an experience that could be shared beyond the classroom.

It was also encouraging to have a tangible example to show younger students and their families what Digital Technologies can offer.

This has influenced how I think about future curriculum planning. I would like to continue creating opportunities for students to work towards authentic outcomes, particularly projects that can be demonstrated, shared or used within the College community.

I want my students to leave Digital Technologies with more than technical skills. I want them to have the confidence to imagine something, work through the challenges of building it and create an outcome that has a genuine purpose for others.

evidence.title: High Expectations, Genuine Care: Learning Through Boarding
evidence.summary: Learning to balance consistent expectations with patience, encouragement and everyday care in Middlemore House.
evidence.impact: I have noticed some girls gradually improve their room standards through reminders and encouragement, while others consistently maintain excellent standards.

sections.title: My role and learning context
sections.text:
As a boarding tutor at Middlemore House, my day-to-day responsibility is to look after the girls and help provide a safe, caring and supportive environment where they can feel at home.

Much of this involves ordinary routines, such as morning and evening roll calls, checking rooms, ensuring students are wearing the correct uniform, reminding them of boarding expectations and being available when they need someone to talk to.

Although these responsibilities may seem small individually, I have come to appreciate how important consistency and attention to detail are in boarding life.

I try to maintain high expectations while remembering that the girls are teenagers learning to manage their own responsibilities, friendships, academic pressures and independence.

I am still learning how to find the right balance between being firm when necessary and showing patience and understanding.

sections.title: Encouraging responsibility and recognising progress
sections.text:
One of my regular duties is checking the girls' rooms. I use an Achieved, Merit and Excellence grading system to recognise room standards and track their progress over time.

I have enjoyed seeing how the girls respond to these expectations. Some consistently maintain excellent standards, while others gradually improve through reminders and encouragement.

I find it particularly rewarding to notice improvement, even when it happens in small steps. I want the girls to feel that their effort matters, not just the final grade.

The photographs I have collected over several weeks help me reflect on how consistent expectations and feedback can encourage students to develop better habits.

This has also reminded me to think carefully about how I communicate expectations. I want the girls to understand that keeping their rooms tidy and following routines is part of learning to take care of themselves and respect the people they live with.

sections.title: Making time for pastoral conversations
sections.text:
Roll call is another important part of my boarding duties. Alongside taking attendance and communicating daily information, I occasionally prepare short presentations or discussions about pastoral topics.

These might focus on wellbeing, relationships, respect, responsibility or the challenges students experience in school and boarding life.

I also enjoy recognising the girls' achievements and progress, whether in their academic work, co-curricular activities or personal development.

I hope these moments help create a positive atmosphere where the girls feel noticed and encouraged.

I am learning that pastoral care does not always require a formal conversation. Sometimes it is simply noticing that someone seems unusually quiet, asking how their day has been or taking a few minutes to listen.

sections.title: Learning through everyday relationships
sections.text:
Working in boarding has allowed me to see a different side of student life from what I usually experience in the classroom.

I have become more aware of the challenges students face when living away from home, managing friendships, keeping up with schoolwork and learning to become more independent.

There are times when I need to remind students of expectations or address behaviour that affects others. These situations are not always easy, and I sometimes reflect afterwards on whether I handled a conversation in the most helpful way.

I am gradually learning that different students respond to different approaches. Some appreciate direct guidance, while others need reassurance, patience or simply an opportunity to explain what is happening.

This experience has helped me better understand manaakitanga, showing care and respect through everyday actions, and whanaungatanga, building relationships and a sense of belonging.

sections.title: An idea inspired by boarding: Luma
sections.text:
My experience as a boarding tutor has also inspired me to think about how technology might support student wellbeing.

Through everyday interactions with the girls, I have become more aware that students sometimes find it difficult to express how they are feeling or recognise when they may need support.

This led me to begin exploring Luma, an idea for a student wellbeing application.

I imagine a simple, welcoming space where students could reflect on their emotions, develop greater awareness of their wellbeing and find information about appropriate support.

It is still an early concept, and I recognise there are many important questions to consider, particularly around privacy, safeguarding and how such a tool would fit within existing pastoral systems.

I would never want technology to replace the relationships and conversations that are so important in boarding.

For me, Luma is simply an idea that has grown from my experiences and my curiosity about whether thoughtful digital design could offer another way to support young people.

sections.title: My reflection
sections.text:
Boarding has become a meaningful part of my professional learning.

It has taught me that looking after students involves both everyday practical responsibilities and being attentive to their individual needs.

I am still developing my confidence in managing expectations, responding to different situations and finding the right words when students need guidance.

I would like to continue improving how I use roll calls to share positive messages, recognise progress and encourage the girls to take responsibility for themselves and their community.

Most importantly, I hope the girls feel that I am someone they can approach, while knowing that I will also encourage them to meet the expectations of boarding life.

What I am learning is that pastoral care often happens through small, consistent actions: being present, noticing changes, following through on expectations and taking the time to listen.

evidence.title: Seeing My Teaching Through Another Pair of Eyes
evidence.context: Peer observations · Computer Science and Year 9 Coding
evidence.summary: What colleagues helped me notice about classroom routines, pacing and how I share my attention across the class.
evidence.need:
I have always believed that we learn a great deal from one another as teachers. But I also know that when I'm busy teaching, it's difficult to see everything happening in my own classroom.

I'm thinking about the student in front of me who needs help, the next part of the lesson, whether everyone understands, and whether we'll have enough time to finish.

Sometimes I leave a lesson feeling that it went really well. Other times, I wonder whether I explained something clearly enough or spent too long helping one student.

Having a colleague observe my teaching gives me another perspective. They notice things I might have missed, both the things that are working and the things I could do differently.

Looking back at my observations from 2025 and 2026, I found the feedback both encouraging and thought-provoking.
evidence.practice:
In 2025, the observation feedback highlighted my classroom organisation, clear expectations and approachable manner with students.

One of the lessons discussed involved bitwise manipulation, which can be quite challenging for students. The notes recognised the way I supported ākonga through the activities and made myself available to those who needed additional help.

I was pleased to read this because I care about making my classroom a place where students feel comfortable asking questions.

But another observation point stayed with me.

When I'm helping someone with a particularly difficult programming problem, it can take several minutes to work through their thinking. During that time, what is happening with the rest of the class?

This made me reflect on something I hadn't always considered carefully enough. Giving one student my full attention is important, but so is making sure everyone else has a clear direction and enough support to continue learning independently.

The 2026 observation offered another perspective.

During a Year 9 Coding lesson, students were developing a maze game. I began by revisiting their previous learning through a quiz, introduced the new activity and gave them time to start exploring it.

Later, I brought their attention back for a demonstration about variables, making connections with concepts they already knew from Mathematics.

My colleague commented that I had explained the activity clearly without overexplaining it. Students were given opportunities to practise the new concepts and then continue developing their projects.

I was happy to hear this because it's something I try to be conscious of in programming lessons. I don't want to spend the whole lesson talking about code. At some point, students need to get their hands on it, experiment and discover things for themselves.
evidence.reflection:
One thing I've learnt is that being open to feedback takes a little humility.

As teachers, we put a lot of ourselves into our lessons. It's natural to feel pleased when someone notices what went well, and perhaps a little uncomfortable when they point out something we could improve.

But I don't want to become the kind of teacher who is so comfortable with my own approach that I stop questioning it.

I believe we learn from one another. I can learn from experienced colleagues, beginning teachers and my own ākonga. Everyone sees the classroom from a different position.

I want to use students' responses at those checkpoints to decide what needs another explanation, then revisit their understanding later. Discussing those responses with a colleague would help me look beyond how smoothly a lesson ran and focus on what students learnt.
evidence.next:
These observations have encouraged me to be more deliberate about three things.

First, I want to continue giving students the freedom to explore and solve problems independently, while providing clearer checkpoints for those who need additional support.

Second, I want to think more carefully about how I distribute my attention, especially in large practical classes. I don't want the students who ask the most questions to be the only ones receiving my help.

Finally, I want to make more time for professional conversations after observations. Not just asking whether the lesson went well, but discussing what students were actually learning, what we noticed and what could be tried differently.

I appreciate colleagues taking the time to observe and share their perspectives. Teaching can sometimes feel quite individual, even when we work in the same department.

Having another teacher in the room reminds me that professional learning doesn't always require a formal workshop or course.

Sometimes, it begins with someone saying, "Have you thought about trying this another way?"

And being willing to listen.
evidence.impact:
What I found interesting was how the observations helped me recognise both strengths and areas for improvement.

The positive feedback reassured me that my classroom routines, relationships with ākonga and practical approach to teaching were supporting their engagement.

I also began thinking more about the quieter students.

A class can look busy. Everyone can have a laptop open and appear to be working. But how do I know they really understand what they're doing?

The feedback made me think about the importance of checking understanding throughout a lesson, not just when a student puts their hand up.

The 2026 observation also reminded me of the value of pacing. Introducing an idea, giving students time to experiment, bringing them back for a short explanation and then allowing them to apply their learning can be more effective than explaining everything at the beginning.

I don't think these observations prove that my teaching has improved in every area. But they have helped me become more aware of the decisions I make and the experiences students may be having.

This made me reflect on something I hadn't always considered carefully enough. Giving one student my full attention is important, but so is making sure everyone else has a clear direction and enough support to continue learning independently.

The 2026 observation offered another perspective.

During a Year 9 Coding lesson, students were developing a maze game. I began by revisiting their previous learning through a quiz, introduced the new activity and gave them time to start exploring it.

Later, I brought their attention back for a demonstration about variables, making connections with concepts they already knew from Mathematics.

My colleague commented that I had explained the activity clearly without overexplaining it. Students were given opportunities to practise the new concepts and then continue developing their projects.

I was happy to hear this because it's something I try to be conscious of in programming lessons. I don't want to spend the whole lesson talking about code. At some point, students need to get their hands on it, experiment and discover things for themselves.

sections.title: What changed
sections.text:
What I found interesting was how the observations helped me recognise both strengths and areas for improvement.

The positive feedback reassured me that my classroom routines, relationships with ākonga and practical approach to teaching were supporting their engagement.

I also began thinking more about the quieter students.

A class can look busy. Everyone can have a laptop open and appear to be working. But how do I know they really understand what they're doing?

The feedback made me think about the importance of checking understanding throughout a lesson, not just when a student puts their hand up.

The 2026 observation also reminded me of the value of pacing. Introducing an idea, giving students time to experiment, bringing them back for a short explanation and then allowing them to apply their learning can be more effective than explaining everything at the beginning.

I don't think these observations prove that my teaching has improved in every area. But they have helped me become more aware of the decisions I make and the experiences students may be having.

sections.title: My reflection and next steps
sections.text:
One thing I've learnt is that being open to feedback takes a little humility.

As teachers, we put a lot of ourselves into our lessons. It's natural to feel pleased when someone notices what went well, and perhaps a little uncomfortable when they point out something we could improve.

But I don't want to become the kind of teacher who is so comfortable with my own approach that I stop questioning it.

I believe we learn from one another. I can learn from experienced colleagues, beginning teachers and my own ākonga. Everyone sees the classroom from a different position.

These observations have encouraged me to be more deliberate about three things.

First, I want to continue giving students the freedom to explore and solve problems independently, while providing clearer checkpoints for those who need additional support.

Second, I want to think more carefully about how I distribute my attention, especially in large practical classes. I don't want the students who ask the most questions to be the only ones receiving my help.

Finally, I want to make more time for professional conversations after observations. Not just asking whether the lesson went well, but discussing what students were actually learning, what we noticed and what could be tried differently.

I appreciate colleagues taking the time to observe and share their perspectives. Teaching can sometimes feel quite individual, even when we work in the same department.

Having another teacher in the room reminds me that professional learning doesn't always require a formal workshop or course.

Sometimes, it begins with someone saying, "Have you thought about trying this another way?"

And being willing to listen.

I want to use students' responses at those checkpoints to decide what needs another explanation, then revisit their understanding later. Discussing those responses with a colleague would help me look beyond how smoothly a lesson ran and focus on what students learnt.

evidence.title: Designing Beyond the Classroom: Learning from Tip Top
evidence.context: NCEA Level 3 Digital Technologies · Authentic project development
evidence.summary: Using a Tip Top factory visit to connect senior digital development with real users, purposeful outcomes and more independent design decisions.
evidence.impact: The project produced student digital outcomes including Ice Cream Buddy, a customisation app, and the digital game Ice Cream Rush.

sections.title: Bringing the real world into curriculum design
sections.text:
One of my goals when designing the NCEA Level 3 Digital Technologies programme was to provide students with opportunities to work on projects that had meaning beyond the classroom.

I wanted students to experience more of the process that designers and developers go through when creating digital outcomes for real users. This includes understanding a problem, researching the context, considering stakeholder needs and making thoughtful decisions throughout development.

With this in mind, I organised a visit to the Tip Top factory, giving students an opportunity to explore a real business environment and use what they learnt to inform the design and development of a digital outcome.

sections.title: Learning from an authentic context
sections.text:
The field trip was an opportunity for students to observe a working environment and think about how digital technologies might respond to genuine needs or opportunities.

Rather than beginning with a predetermined product, I wanted students to approach the experience with curiosity.

What challenges might exist in this environment? Who would use a proposed digital solution? What would make an outcome useful, practical and appropriate for its intended audience?

I hoped the visit would encourage students to look beyond the technical features of a product and consider its purpose.

It also gave them a chance to connect their classroom learning with the wider world and see how their programming and design skills might be applied outside school.

sections.title: Designing and developing purposeful outcomes
sections.text:
Following the visit, the intention was for students to use their observations and research to inform their individual digital projects.

I wanted them to work through the design and development process, from identifying a need or opportunity to planning, building, testing and refining an outcome.

An important part of my curriculum design was allowing students to make their own decisions rather than providing everyone with the same project brief or finished solution.

This required me to think about how much guidance to provide. Students needed enough structure to understand the expectations of NCEA Level 3, but also the independence to investigate ideas, make technical decisions and respond to feedback.

I wanted assessment evidence to emerge naturally from the development process, with students explaining why they made particular decisions and how their outcomes responded to the needs of their intended users.

sections.title: Reflecting on my role as a teacher
sections.text:
Planning a project around a real-world context made me reflect on the difference between teaching technical skills and helping students apply those skills purposefully.

In a classroom exercise, the problem and expected outcome are often already defined. In an authentic project, students may need to spend more time understanding the context before deciding what to create.

I have found that this requires a different kind of support from me as a teacher.

Instead of always providing answers, I want to become better at asking questions that help students clarify their thinking, justify their choices and evaluate their work.

I also recognise that open-ended projects can be challenging. Students may have ambitious ideas that need to be refined into realistic outcomes, particularly within the available time and their current technical capabilities.

As I continue developing the programme, I want to improve how I support students through this early stage of defining a problem and establishing a manageable project scope.

sections.title: What I would like to improve
sections.text:
Reflecting on the field trip and project design, I would like to strengthen the connection between the experience outside school and the learning that follows.

For future projects, I would prepare more focused observation questions and encourage students to document possible user needs, constraints and design opportunities during a visit.

I would also like to build more structured opportunities for stakeholder feedback and technical testing into the development process.

Another consideration is helping students distinguish between an interesting idea and a purposeful digital outcome. I want them to become more confident in explaining not only what they have created, but why it is needed and how they know it meets its intended purpose.

sections.title: My reflection
sections.text:
The Tip Top project has encouraged me to think more carefully about how I connect curriculum content, assessment requirements and authentic learning experiences.

I enjoy teaching programming and digital development, but I also want students to recognise that these skills are tools for understanding problems and creating solutions.

Organising a field trip and designing a project around a real organisation was an opportunity for me to explore a more authentic approach to senior Digital Technologies.

I am still learning how to balance student independence with the structure and guidance needed for successful project development.

My hope is that students leave the course not only knowing how to develop a digital product, but also understanding how to investigate a real need, make informed design decisions and create something purposeful for others.

evidence.title: Small Steps Towards Cultural Confidence
evidence.context: Te reo Māori, tikanga Māori and culturally responsive teaching
evidence.summary: Reflecting on my cultural understanding, the questions raised by cultural game design, and practical steps I want to take in my teaching.
evidence.need:
One area of my teaching practice that I would like to develop further is my understanding and use of te reo Māori and tikanga Māori.

I recognise that I am still at an early stage of this learning. While I understand the importance of honouring Aotearoa New Zealand's bicultural foundations, I would like to become more confident in how I put this understanding into practice in my classroom.

As someone who has experienced learning and working across different cultural environments, I appreciate that language, identity and belonging are important parts of a student's experience at school.

I am conscious that culturally responsive teaching involves more than learning a few words or including cultural references in a lesson. It requires listening, developing understanding and considering whose perspectives are represented in the learning experiences I design.
evidence.practice:
One opportunity for me to explore this has been through curriculum design.

In my Year 11 Digital Innovation programme, students have opportunities to design and develop digital outcomes for an intended audience. In our cultural game design project, students are encouraged to explore cultural identities and traditions and consider how these can be represented through interactive media.

This has made me reflect on how digital technologies can provide opportunities for students to share stories, communicate identity and learn from one another.

It has also raised important questions for me about cultural representation. When students create a game inspired by a culture, how do we help them represent it respectfully and accurately? How do we encourage them to research, seek appropriate feedback and avoid relying on stereotypes?

These are questions I would like to explore more thoughtfully in my future teaching.

I also recognise that including Māori perspectives requires more than treating them as one option among many cultures. I want to develop a better understanding of how mātauranga Māori, te reo Māori and tikanga Māori can be included appropriately and meaningfully within Digital Technologies education.
evidence.reflection:
I do not yet feel confident enough to say that te reo Māori and tikanga Māori are naturally embedded throughout my teaching.

However, I recognise that this is an important part of my professional growth, and I want to take responsibility for improving my understanding.

I am not yet confident in my use of te reo Māori, and I know I have more to learn about tikanga Māori and te ao Māori.

Moving forward, I would like to practise pronunciation more regularly, become more comfortable using everyday expressions and seek opportunities to deepen my understanding of Māori perspectives in education.

For me, the next step is to move beyond good intentions and begin developing consistent habits that I can reflect on and improve.

My goal is not simply to include more Māori words in my lessons, but to become a teacher who better understands and respects the language, identity and cultural knowledge of Aotearoa New Zealand, and who can reflect that understanding more meaningfully in my teaching practice.
evidence.next:
Rather than trying to make large changes before I have developed sufficient understanding, I would like to begin with manageable and consistent steps.

I want to improve my pronunciation and confidence when using everyday te reo Māori, particularly greetings, classroom instructions and common educational terms.

I would also like to learn more about tikanga relevant to school life, including how to participate respectfully in pōwhiri, mihi and other occasions.

In curriculum planning, I want to become more deliberate about including authentic Māori perspectives where they genuinely connect with the learning objectives, and seek guidance when I am uncertain.

I recognise that this learning will take time, and I would value opportunities to learn from colleagues, professional development and appropriate Māori educational resources.

evidence.title: Listening to Student Voice: Refining Our Year 9 Coding Programme
evidence.context: Year 9 Coding · VR/AR, programming and student feedback
evidence.summary: Using Year 9 student feedback to review pacing, support and the progression from introductory VR/AR activities to independent creative work.
evidence.need:
Year 9 Coding is a short introductory course that Richard and I teach together, each bringing different areas of expertise.

I teach the VR/AR design component, where students explore immersive environments and create interactive experiences using Delightex. Richard teaches Python programming and Raspberry Pi, introducing students to coding, physical computing and how software interacts with hardware.

I enjoy this arrangement because it gives students opportunities to experience different aspects of Digital Technologies before deciding whether they would like to continue studying the subject.

However, with a limited number of weeks available, we need to make careful decisions about how much students can realistically learn and develop within each component.
evidence.practice:
I particularly enjoyed reading comments about students creating their own games and sharing their projects with others.

One student identified making a parkour horror game in Delightex and playing classmates' games as a highlight of the course.

This reflects something I value in my teaching: giving students opportunities to move beyond following instructions and make creative decisions of their own.

At the same time, not all students enjoyed the VR/AR activities equally. Some identified Delightex, the AR Merge Cube activities or VR itself as their least favourite part of the course.

I think this is useful feedback. It encourages me to consider whether the learning activities have a clear enough purpose, whether the instructions are accessible and whether students have sufficient time to become comfortable with the technology before beginning independent work.

I would like to improve the progression from introductory VR/AR exploration to creating an interactive outcome, while allowing students some choice in the type of experience they develop.
evidence.reflection:
Reading the student feedback has been a valuable opportunity to look at the Year 9 programme from the students' perspective.

I was encouraged that many students enjoyed the course and felt supported, but the responses also reminded me that engagement does not automatically mean every student has experienced the right level of challenge or enough time to learn.

My main priority is to review the pacing and structure of the VR/AR component, particularly how students move from introductory activities towards independent creative development.

I would also like to discuss the findings with Richard so we can consider how the different parts of the course connect and whether the overall programme provides a balanced introduction to coding.

For future rotations, I hope to collect student feedback more consistently and use it alongside classroom observations and examples of student work.

My biggest learning is that student voice gives me an opportunity to question my own assumptions. sections.title: A course designed to explore different technologies
sections.text:
Year 9 Coding is a short introductory course that Richard and I teach together, each bringing different areas of expertise.

I teach the VR/AR design component, where students explore immersive environments and create interactive experiences using Delightex. Richard teaches Python programming and Raspberry Pi, introducing students to coding, physical computing and how software interacts with hardware.

I enjoy this arrangement because it gives students opportunities to experience different aspects of Digital Technologies before deciding whether they would like to continue studying the subject.

However, with a limited number of weeks available, we need to make careful decisions about how much students can realistically learn and develop within each component.

sections.title: What students told us
sections.text:
At the end of the course, we collected student feedback to better understand their learning experiences.

The responses were encouraging. Of the 29 students who answered the enjoyment question, 23 agreed or strongly agreed that Year 9 Coding was a fun course. Twenty-four out of 30 students also agreed that they felt supported when they needed help.

I was pleased to see these results because I want students' first experiences of coding to be positive, particularly those who may have little previous programming experience.

The written comments also showed a wide range of interests. Some students particularly enjoyed Python programming and working with Raspberry Pi, while others preferred designing games and experimenting with VR.

It was interesting to see that the same activities sometimes appeared in both the most-enjoyed and least-enjoyed responses.

This reminded me that students experience learning differently. An activity that is exciting for one student may feel challenging, confusing or less engaging for another.

sections.title: Reflecting on the VR/AR component
sections.text:
I particularly enjoyed reading comments about students creating their own games and sharing their projects with others.

One student identified making a parkour horror game in Delightex and playing classmates' games as a highlight of the course.

This reflects something I value in my teaching: giving students opportunities to move beyond following instructions and make creative decisions of their own.

At the same time, not all students enjoyed the VR/AR activities equally. Some identified Delightex, the AR Merge Cube activities or VR itself as their least favourite part of the course.

I think this is useful feedback. It encourages me to consider whether the learning activities have a clear enough purpose, whether the instructions are accessible and whether students have sufficient time to become comfortable with the technology before beginning independent work.

I would like to improve the progression from introductory VR/AR exploration to creating an interactive outcome, while allowing students some choice in the type of experience they develop.

sections.title: The challenge of pacing
sections.text:
The area that stood out most clearly was the pace of the course.

Although most students enjoyed the programme, only half of the respondents agreed that the pace was appropriate.

Some comments suggested that activities felt rushed, while others indicated that certain topics continued for too long or were difficult to follow.

This is something I want to take seriously when planning the next rotation.

Because students experience several different technologies in a short period, there is a risk of introducing too much content without leaving enough time for practice and consolidation.

I would like to work with Richard to review the time allocated to each component, identify the most important learning outcomes and consider how transitions between topics could be improved.

For my VR/AR lessons, I want to make sure students have enough time to understand the tools, practise essential skills and complete a meaningful creative activity, rather than rushing to cover every available feature.

sections.title: Supporting different starting points
sections.text:
Another useful finding was that students had different experiences of difficulty.

Some found Python challenging, while others particularly enjoyed programming and wanted to learn more. Similar differences appeared in feedback about Raspberry Pi and immersive design.

This reminded me that Year 9 students bring different levels of confidence and previous experience.

For future rotations, I would like to provide more structured introductory activities, clearer examples and optional extension challenges.

Within the VR/AR component, this could mean ensuring everyone can successfully create a basic interactive environment before introducing more advanced possibilities for students who want additional challenge.

I also want to continue giving students opportunities to explore independently, make mistakes and learn from one another.

sections.title: Helping students discover their interests
sections.text:
One of the purposes of Year 9 Coding is to introduce students to what further study in Digital Technologies could involve.

I found this interesting because nearly half the respondents were still unsure about continuing.

I do not think this necessarily reflects dissatisfaction with the course. Students' subject choices can be influenced by many factors, and the survey does not explain their reasons.

However, it does encourage me to think about how we communicate the possibilities of studying Digital Technologies beyond Year 9.

The written responses showed continued interest in programming, robotics, Raspberry Pi and game development.

I would like to make these connections more visible, helping students understand how the different experiences in our course can lead towards more advanced projects and future learning pathways.
