evidence.title: Different Starting Points, Shared Ambition
evidence.context: Year 11 Digital Technologies · Cultural Game Design
evidence.summary: Using game design to explore culture, listen to stakeholders and give students room to create something meaningful.
evidence.need:
Coming from a design background, I've always believed that what we create should have meaning.

When planning our Year 11 game design project, I wanted students to do more than learn how to make characters move, create animations or build a playable game.

I wanted them to think about the people they were designing for.

King's is a diverse community, and our ākonga come from different cultural backgrounds, with their own stories, traditions, languages and experiences.

I thought, why not make this part of our learning?

Rather than giving everyone the same game to build, I wanted students to explore culture through something they already find engaging: video games.

The challenge was to create an original game celebrating a particular culture, with students and families attending the College's Open Day or Options Afternoon as the intended audience.
evidence.practice:
I developed a Cultural Game Design project for NCEA Achievement Standard 92005, where students were asked to research, design, develop and test an original game that represented their chosen cultural context.

I wanted students to understand that culture is much more than food, clothing or traditional symbols. It includes language, values, beliefs, stories, experiences and ways of life.

An important part of the task was asking students to engage with stakeholders.

I didn't want them to simply search online, collect a few images and decide that they understood someone else's culture.

I wanted them to ask questions, listen and consider whether the people they were representing would recognise themselves in the final outcome.

This was also an opportunity to discuss respectful representation. A cultural reference might look interesting in a game, but does it have meaning? Is it appropriate to use? Have we understood its significance?

I provided examples of culturally inspired games, including Never Alone, which was developed through collaboration with Alaska Native storytellers and artists. This helped illustrate how cultural knowledge and modern game development can work together.

At the same time, students needed to develop the technical skills to create a working game.

We used Construct 3, beginning with smaller projects such as a car game, maze game and platformer before students began developing their own outcomes.

This gave them opportunities to learn game mechanics, event-based programming, collision detection, animation and interaction before applying those skills independently.

Students were also expected to plan their ideas, develop storyboards, test gameplay, gather stakeholder feedback and document improvements.

I liked that the assessment valued not just the finished game, but the thinking and decisions behind it.

I also included te reo Māori in the project brief through headings such as Kupu Arataki, Hei Mahi and Tāpaetanga. I want to continue developing my use of te reo Māori in ways that are meaningful rather than decorative.
evidence.reflection:
This project reminded me why I enjoy teaching Digital Technologies.

I love seeing students take an idea and turn it into something real. But I also want them to understand that creating technology comes with responsibilities.

When we design something for other people, we need to listen to them.

For me, this connects with whanaungatanga, building relationships and understanding the people we work with, and manaakitanga, showing care and respect in how we represent others.

It also made me reflect on my own understanding of culturally responsive teaching.

I don't think it is enough to include a Māori word, a cultural image or an international theme in a lesson.

I want to understand whose knowledge we are using, whose perspectives are represented and whether students have genuine opportunities to bring their own identities into the learning.

I am still developing my understanding of te ao Māori and tikanga Māori. If students choose to work with Māori stories, symbols or mātauranga Māori, I want to ensure that this is approached respectfully, with appropriate guidance and engagement with the people who hold that knowledge.

I want to look closely at the development presentations and design changes to see how students applied the foundations from the smaller Construct 3 projects. Their explanations of technical decisions and responses to stakeholder feedback would help me judge where cultural understanding and technical learning need more time.
evidence.next:
One challenge I noticed in planning the project was balancing the time students needed for cultural research with the technical demands of learning a new game engine.

I don't want cultural understanding to become something students rush through before beginning the coding.

If I teach this unit again, I would like to spend more time on stakeholder engagement at the beginning and build in clearer opportunities for students to explain how feedback has changed their designs.

I would also like to gather more student voice about what they learnt from exploring culture through game development.

Above all, this project reflects something I strongly believe as a teacher.

I have high expectations for all my ākonga, but I don't believe they need to create the same thing to demonstrate their ability.

Their different backgrounds, interests and experiences are not obstacles to learning.

They are things we can learn from.
evidence.impact:
What I enjoyed about this project was the opportunity for students to approach the same technical challenge from different starting points.

Students could draw on their own interests, cultural connections and research rather than simply reproduce a game I had demonstrated.

The project also made me think differently about what successful learning looks like in Digital Technologies.

A technically impressive game is not necessarily a well-designed game if it doesn't communicate its intended meaning or meet the needs of its audience.

I wanted students to begin asking themselves questions beyond "Does my game work?"

Who is this game for? What am I trying to communicate? Have I represented the culture thoughtfully? What did my stakeholder think, and what should I change?

These questions matter just as much as debugging code or improving gameplay.

The final projects and development presentations provide opportunities to look at how students interpreted the brief, made design decisions and responded to feedback.

evidence.title: Finding Their Feet: Supporting Year 11 Girls at King's
evidence.summary: Supporting girls as they join King's, balancing academic expectations with friendships, wellbeing and a growing sense of belonging.
evidence.impact: Mentoring has helped me recognise that academically capable students can still need reassurance and time to adjust to a new school.

sections.title: Understanding their different starting points
sections.text:
Mentoring Year 11 girls at King's has helped me appreciate the challenges they face when joining a new school.

For our girls, Year 11 is their first year at King's. While some boys have already spent two years at the College, and some have come through King's Prep and are familiar with a similar school system, the girls are learning to navigate a new environment at the same time as beginning their senior school journey.

I have noticed that some girls can feel disadvantaged by this difference. They are expected to settle into senior academic expectations while learning the College's routines, finding their way around, forming friendships and discovering where they belong.

For Middlemore girls in boarding, there is another layer of adjustment as they learn to manage life away from home.

This has reminded me that students who are in the same year level may not necessarily be starting from the same place.

sections.title: Supporting academic progress and personal expectations
sections.text:
One of my responsibilities as a mentor is to monitor the girls' academic progress and check how they are managing their learning.

I have noticed that many of the girls set high expectations for themselves. They want to achieve good results, participate in activities, maintain friendships and make the most of their opportunities at King's.

Sometimes these expectations can create additional pressure, particularly while they are still settling into a new school.

During mentor conversations, I try to look beyond assessment grades and understand how each student is feeling about her progress.

We discuss academic goals, study habits, challenges and the support they may need. I also encourage them to recognise improvements rather than focusing only on what they have not yet achieved.

I am learning that mentoring is not always about encouraging students to do more. Sometimes it is about helping them find balance and recognise that adjusting to a new environment takes time.

sections.title: Friendships, belonging and settling into school life
sections.text:
Another aspect I have become more conscious of is the importance of friendships and social connections.

Many of the girls enjoy spending time with friends and being involved in the social life of the College. For students who are new to King's, developing these relationships can be an important part of feeling comfortable and confident at school.

I have learnt not to underestimate how much a sense of belonging can influence a student's experience.

A student might be managing her academic work well but still feel uncertain about friendships or finding her place within the wider school community.

During mentoring conversations, I try to give the girls space to talk about these aspects of their lives as well as their academic progress.

I also enjoy our group mentor activities designed by Grant, which provide opportunities for the girls to spend time together discussing topics relevant to their wellbeing and academic learning.

sections.title: Celebrating success and recognising growth
sections.text:
One of the most enjoyable parts of mentoring is celebrating the girls' achievements.

I like recognising success, but I also try to acknowledge progress in confidence, organisation, participation and personal development.

For a student who is new to the College, joining a new activity, making friends or becoming more comfortable asking for help can be meaningful achievements. I like to help them set realistic termly goals and reflect on them together. I want the girls to understand that success is not measured only by grades. Sometimes the most encouraging conversations happen when a student begins to recognise how far she has come since the beginning of the year.

sections.title: What mentoring has taught me
sections.text:
This experience has encouraged me to be more patient and attentive to the different needs of students.

I have learnt that the transition into Year 11 at King's can be quite different for girls joining the College for the first time, compared with students who are already familiar with the school.

It has also reminded me that academically capable and motivated students can still need reassurance, guidance and time to adjust.

As a mentor, I cannot solve every challenge they face, but I can try to be someone who listens, checks in regularly and helps them find appropriate support.

I have also developed a greater appreciation for whanaungatanga, building relationships and belonging, and manaakitanga, showing care and respect through everyday interactions.

sections.title: My reflection and next steps
sections.text:
Looking ahead, I would like to make my mentoring more responsive to the transition challenges experienced by Year 11 girls.

I want to continue monitoring academic progress while also making time to discuss friendships, wellbeing, participation and the pressures students place on themselves.

I would also like to help the girls set realistic goals, revisit their progress and celebrate both their achievements and the small steps they make towards feeling settled.

My biggest learning is that being a senior student does not necessarily mean feeling established or confident. For many of our Year 11 girls, they are still finding their feet. I hope my role as a mentor can make that transition a little easier by helping them feel supported, recognised and connected to the College community.

evidence.title: Rethinking Year 11: Bridging Computer Science and Digital Technologies
evidence.summary: Redesigning Year 11 to combine Computer Science foundations with Python programming and creative game development, while reviewing the balance between breadth and depth.
evidence.impact: The redesigned Year 11 Digital Innovation programme combines IGCSE content with Python and Construct 3 projects, giving students experience of both theoretical and practical pathways.

sections.title: Rethinking the purpose of Year 11
sections.text:
When I joined King's College in 2024, our Year 11 programme followed Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science. The course provided students with a theoretical and programming foundation, but I began to reflect on whether it offered enough opportunities to experience the creative and practical side of Digital Technologies.

I felt that Year 11 was an important opportunity for students to explore different aspects of the subject before making their senior course selections. Not every student knows whether they prefer theoretical Computer Science, programming or creative digital development, and I wanted the course to give them a meaningful introduction to these possibilities.

This thinking led me to redesign the programme for 2025 and continue refining it in 2026.

sections.title: Designing a combined pathway
sections.text:
The redesigned course, Year 11 Digital Innovation, brings together Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science content and NCEA Level 1 Digital Technologies projects.

The intention was to provide students with both academic foundations and opportunities to apply their learning through practical development.

In the first part of the programme, students explore IGCSE topics including data representation, networking, computer hardware and software, Boolean logic, databases, and problem-solving.

These topics help students understand how digital systems work and develop the computational thinking needed for further study.

Programming is introduced through flowcharts, pseudocode and Python, with students learning to use variables, selection, iteration, functions and data structures to solve problems.

The practical component then gives students opportunities to apply these skills through two projects.

The first is a Python programming project aligned with NCEA AS92004, where students identify a problem, develop a program and provide evidence of testing and debugging.

The second is a game design project aligned with NCEA AS92005, where students use Construct 3 to develop an interactive 2D game. This introduces another dimension of digital development, including game mechanics, user experience, visual design, testing and stakeholder feedback.

I particularly enjoy this part of the programme because students can see their ideas gradually become working digital outcomes.

My hope is that experiencing both theoretical study and practical development gives students a better understanding of what they might enjoy pursuing in Years 12 and 13.

sections.title: Balancing academic depth with creative exploration
sections.text:
One of the challenges I have encountered in designing this programme is finding the right balance between breadth and depth.

The curriculum covers a substantial amount of IGCSE content, while also expecting students to develop programming confidence and complete two practical projects.

The 2026 assessment structure reflects this balance, with 50% allocated to the IGCSE final examination and 25% to each practical project.

Although I value giving students experience of both pathways, I have been reflecting on whether the teaching sequence allows enough time for students to consolidate their knowledge before moving on.

For example, understanding programming structures in theory is not the same as being able to use them independently in a Python application. Students need time to practise, make mistakes, debug and develop confidence.

I also want to strengthen the connections between the different units. Rather than students seeing data representation, programming and game development as separate topics, I would like them to recognise how these concepts work together.

This has encouraged me to think more carefully about how I sequence lessons and revisit foundational concepts throughout the year.

sections.title: Using assessment and student experience to inform improvement
sections.text:
The 2026 course includes topic tests, practical assessments and a final examination.

These provide different opportunities to evaluate students' understanding. Written tests can help identify gaps in theoretical knowledge, while project work offers evidence of students' ability to apply programming, design and problem-solving skills.

I would like to make better use of these different forms of evidence when reviewing the curriculum.

For example, if a student performs well in a practical game project but struggles with examination questions, I want to understand whether the difficulty relates to subject knowledge, written explanation or examination technique.

Similarly, if a student understands programming concepts but finds independent development challenging, I need to consider whether more structured practice is required before beginning a larger project.

I also want to gather student feedback about the parts of the programme they find engaging, challenging or most helpful when considering future subject choices.

My aim is to make curriculum decisions based on learning evidence rather than assumptions about what students prefer.

sections.title: Looking ahead to the new national curriculum
sections.text:
The release of New Zealand's proposed senior Technology curriculum in October 2026 has made this reflection particularly timely.

The proposed Year 11 Digital Technologies pathway brings together computational thinking, Python programming, digital media and artificial intelligence, while Years 12 and 13 introduce separate Computer Science and Digital Media pathways.

I was interested to see how closely this direction relates to the thinking behind our redesigned Year 11 course.

However, it also encourages me to reconsider how the programme could become more coherent, rather than continuing to organise it primarily around IGCSE theory and separate NCEA projects.

For future curriculum development, I would like to investigate an approach where students learn core Computer Science concepts and progressively apply them through purposeful digital outcomes.

I am also interested in introducing foundational AI knowledge and responsible use in ways that build naturally on programming, data representation and computational thinking.

The challenge will be maintaining the academic rigour needed for students continuing into Cambridge AS Computer Science while also preparing those interested in Digital Media and other practical development pathways.

I think this will require careful planning, collaboration and a clear understanding of the knowledge and skills students need at each stage.

sections.title: My reflection and next steps
sections.text:
Redesigning the Year 11 curriculum has been a valuable learning experience for me.

It has helped me think more deeply about the purpose of a junior-to-senior transition course and the importance of giving students opportunities to discover their interests.

I still believe there is value in combining Computer Science foundations with creative project development. However, I recognise that covering more content does not necessarily mean students develop deeper understanding.

Moving forward, I want to review the programme's teaching sequence, analyse assessment results, gather student feedback and examine how students progress into senior courses.

I would also like to explore how smaller programming and interactive development activities could connect theory and practice more naturally before students begin their larger projects.

My biggest learning is that Year 11 should give students both a strong foundation and a clearer sense of direction. I want them to understand how digital technologies work, experience the satisfaction of creating something themselves and make informed choices about their future learning.

evidence.title: From Assessment to Curriculum Design
evidence.context: Cambridge AS Computer Science · Curriculum development
evidence.summary: Using my Cambridge AS results to rethink formative assessment, independent practice and the learning purpose behind Nibble and interactive resources.
evidence.need:
Reviewing the November 2025 Cambridge AS Computer Science results encouraged me to look more closely at my teaching and how I could improve the learning experience for the following year.

I was pleased to see strong achievement among some students, but I was also conscious of the variation across the results. It made me question whether I was providing enough opportunities for students to practise independently, recognise their misconceptions and receive support before the final examinations.

I wanted to use these results as more than a measure of achievement. I wanted them to inform how I design the curriculum.
evidence.practice:
As I review my Cambridge AS programme in 2026, one priority is to make formative assessment a more consistent part of the teaching sequence.

I want to introduce regular retrieval quizzes, short pseudocode exercises and Cambridge-style questions throughout the teaching sequence. These will help me identify gaps in understanding earlier and adjust my teaching before students move on to more complex topics.

I also want to reconsider how I introduce programming concepts. Rather than moving too quickly from worked examples to independent programming tasks, I would like students to spend more time tracing algorithms, predicting outputs, explaining their reasoning and gradually building complete solutions.

Another area I want to improve is differentiation. The results reminded me that students progress at different rates, even within the same class. I want to provide more opportunities for students who need additional practice without limiting the challenge available to those who are ready to move ahead.
evidence.reflection:
Looking back, the most valuable part of reviewing the 2025 results has been recognising that assessment should influence what happens next in my classroom.

Although I was encouraged by the strong achievements of some students, I want to understand how I can better support those who find the course challenging.

This has encouraged me to rethink the teaching sequence, plan more regular formative assessment and explore how interactive learning resources could support independent practice.

It has also given greater purpose to my development of Nibble, connecting my interest in software development with a genuine teaching challenge.

My goal is to create a Cambridge AS Computer Science programme where students have more opportunities to explore, practise, make mistakes and improve throughout the year, rather than discovering gaps in their understanding only when they sit the final examination.
evidence.next:
I recognise that creating more interactive resources does not automatically lead to better learning.

As I develop and introduce these approaches, I want to evaluate whether they are making a difference.

I plan to use diagnostic assessments, short formative quizzes, student feedback and performance on unfamiliar Cambridge-style questions to identify whether students are developing stronger understanding and greater independence.

I would also like to compare future examination results with the 2025 outcomes, while recognising that differences between cohorts need to be considered.

This reflection has also influenced a personal development project I have started planning called Nibble, an interactive Cambridge Computer Science learning platform.

The idea came from a question I have been asking myself: How can I give students more opportunities to practise and receive useful feedback when I cannot be beside every student?

I envisage Nibble as a place where students can select a syllabus topic, work through structured questions and revisit concepts they find difficult.

I am particularly interested in exploring how AI might eventually support this process through personalised hints and guiding questions. evidence.title: Exploring Swift Playgrounds
evidence.context: Apple Education · Swift and Swift Playgrounds
evidence.summary: Building a travel app at an Apple workshop gave me a fresh perspective on learning to code and possibilities for programming on iPads.
evidence.need:
I've always enjoyed exploring different ways of teaching programming, especially when creativity is involved.

I had previously worked with Swift using Xcode, so the programming language wasn't completely new to me. However, I was curious about Swift Playgrounds and how it could make coding more accessible to students.

Many of our ākonga use iPads, and I wondered whether there might be opportunities for them to experience programming and app development using devices they already have.
evidence.practice:
I attended an Apple professional learning workshop led by Steph Worladge, where we explored Swift programming and Swift Playgrounds.

We revisited programming concepts such as functions, arrays, loops, dictionaries, conditional expressions and the differences between structures and classes.

During the workshop, I created a travel app. I really enjoyed going through the process of building something myself, experimenting with the code and seeing the app take shape.

There were moments when things didn't work as expected, and I had to go back and check my syntax. Even with programming experience, I still make mistakes when learning or revisiting a language. It was a nice reminder of what my own ākonga experience when they're learning to code.

What interested me most wasn't necessarily learning another programming language. It was seeing how Swift Playgrounds could provide a different entry point into coding, particularly for younger students.

We also discussed skills that go beyond programming, such as problem-solving, teamwork, communication, curiosity and understanding users' needs.

I enjoyed connecting with other educators too. Hearing different ideas and approaches is always refreshing, especially when so much of our everyday work happens within our own classrooms and departments.
evidence.reflection:
I really enjoyed being a learner again.

Although I was familiar with many of the programming concepts, experiencing them through a different tool made me think about how students encounter coding for the first time.

Sometimes we become comfortable with the tools we already use. This workshop reminded me that there are always other approaches worth exploring.

Before trying an app development activity, I would identify the concepts it should help students learn and how their explanations and code would show their understanding. That would give me a clearer basis for deciding whether a different tool adds something useful to the learning.
evidence.next:
I haven't introduced Swift Playgrounds into my teaching yet, and I don't want to change the curriculum simply because I've discovered something new.

For now, it is another resource I can draw on.

In the future, I would like to explore whether Swift Playgrounds could fit into our junior Digital Technologies programme, perhaps through a short app development activity. With many students already using iPads, it could be an interesting way to introduce programming without requiring a traditional computer lab.

I also want to keep connecting with other teachers and learning from their experiences.

This is what I enjoy about professional learning. Sometimes I come away with something I can use tomorrow. Other times, I come away with an idea that may become useful much later.

Either way, I've added something to the resources I can draw on.
evidence.impact:
The workshop didn't immediately change my curriculum, but it certainly gave me something to think about.

I already teach programming through Python and other development tools. Swift Playgrounds showed me another possibility, particularly for junior ākonga who may find the idea of developing their own app exciting.

I liked the accessibility of the iPad environment and the opportunity for students to create something practical while learning programming concepts.

I also learnt about initiatives such as the Swift Student Challenge, which gave me another avenue to explore for students who want to take their coding further.

evidence.title: From Understanding AI to Building With It
evidence.context: AI teaching, professional learning and independent development
evidence.summary: My journey from teaching the foundations of AI to exploring how to build applications that support students’ thinking.
evidence.need:
My interest in AI didn't begin with ChatGPT or Lauren's professional development session.

I had already taught Artificial Intelligence as a Computer Science concept in NCEA Level 2 Digital Technologies, preparing my ākonga for the AS91898 external examination in 2025.

I really enjoyed teaching this topic because it gave students an opportunity to understand what is happening behind the technology they increasingly use every day.

We explored the foundations of AI, including the difference between traditional programming and systems that learn from data. We looked at weak and strong AI, the Turing Test, machine learning, supervised and unsupervised learning, neural networks, decision trees and natural language processing (NLP).

We also explored how AI systems are trained, how the quality of training data influences their performance, and why bias, reliability and limitations matter.

I wanted students to move beyond simply recognising examples of AI. We investigated how it works in real situations, from recommendation systems and chatbots to autonomous vehicles and healthcare.

An important part of the learning was evaluating AI critically. We discussed hallucinations, ethical concerns, bias, accountability and how AI systems might need to evolve to remain effective and trustworthy.

Preparing students for an NCEA external examination meant they needed more than definitions. They had to explain how the technology worked, apply Computer Science knowledge to unfamiliar situations and discuss its wider implications.

I enjoyed seeing their understanding develop and helping them prepare to communicate that knowledge independently in their external assessment.

That experience gave me a strong foundation in the underlying concepts of AI. But it also made me increasingly curious about the practical side.

I understood the principles behind many AI systems. What would it take for me to start building applications using them?
evidence.practice:
Lauren's PD on AI and Cognitive Science in Term 3, 2026 was an important moment in this journey.

The session explored cognitive offloading and the difference between using AI as a replacement for thinking and using it as a thinking partner.

The Think → AI → Think approach particularly resonated with me.

I had already taught students about how AI systems work, their strengths and their limitations. But Lauren's session made me think more deeply about how we should design learning experiences around this technology.

I started asking myself a different question.

Could I build an AI learning tool that supports the thinking process rather than simply providing answers?

That question encouraged me to begin exploring AI engineering more seriously.

With my existing background in programming, web development, game design and VR/AR teaching, I had a foundation in designing and developing digital outcomes. I wanted to extend those skills into AI-powered applications.

I began exploring large language models (LLMs), application programming interfaces (APIs), JSON structured outputs, embeddings, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and workflow automation.

What interested me was understanding how these technologies connect.

For example, an LLM provides language understanding and generation capabilities, while an API allows a software application to communicate with the model.

RAG offers a way to retrieve relevant information from a knowledge base and provide it as context for an AI response. Structured outputs allow information to be returned in a predictable format that software can process.

I find this fascinating because it connects Computer Science theory with practical product development.

I also began thinking about the limitations. An AI system may generate an answer that sounds convincing but is incorrect. An educational application needs reliable content, appropriate safeguards, testing and meaningful human oversight.

These are not entirely new concerns to me because I have taught AI ethics and limitations before. What is new is learning how to address them when designing an application myself.
evidence.reflection:
What I've enjoyed most is being able to connect something I already know and teach with an entirely new area of learning.

I feel confident discussing the core concepts of AI because I have taught them, explored real-world examples and prepared students for external assessment.

But AI engineering is a different challenge, and I am still learning.

There are new tools, programming techniques, frameworks and design considerations to understand. I find myself researching, experimenting and occasionally getting things wrong.

I actually enjoy that part of the process.

It reminds me of my own teaching philosophy. I want my ākonga to be curious, to try difficult things and to see mistakes as part of learning. I need to be willing to do the same.

I believe we learn from one another. Even with my teaching experience and technical knowledge, there is still so much I can learn from other teachers, developers and the wider education community.

As I develop future AI learning activities, I want to make permitted AI use clear and check what students can explain and evaluate independently. Their own responses, including how they question reliability and bias, would help me judge whether the activity supports their thinking rather than simply produces a polished answer.
evidence.next:
Looking ahead, I see several opportunities.

One is curriculum innovation, particularly as AI becomes more prominent in the Digital Technologies and Computer Science curriculum.

Another is developing and evaluating practical educational applications that could support students and teachers.

I am also interested in supporting colleagues through hands-on professional learning. Beyond introductory AI literacy and prompting, I would love to explore subject-specific applications, AI-supported workflows and opportunities for teachers to create useful tools for their own practice.

I don't see myself as someone who already knows everything about AI.

I see myself as a Computer Science teacher with a solid foundation, a genuine passion for technology and a willingness to keep learning.

My experience teaching AI gave me theoretical understanding. Lauren's PD encouraged me to think more critically about how AI should support learning. My independent exploration is helping me discover how I might turn these ideas into practical applications.

I want to keep learning, keep building and hopefully bring some of that excitement back into my classroom.
evidence.impact:
I think the biggest change has been moving from understanding AI as a Computer Science concept towards exploring AI as something I can develop with.

Teaching AS91898 gave me valuable knowledge of how AI systems learn, operate and affect society.

My more recent exploration has introduced another layer: how to integrate these technologies into applications that respond to real needs.

I've also started looking at the upcoming changes to New Zealand's Digital Technologies and Computer Science curriculum with genuine excitement.

I see an opportunity to bring together theoretical understanding, programming, computational thinking and practical AI development.

I would love students to learn not only what machine learning or neural networks are, but also how AI services can become part of a larger software system.

At the same time, Lauren's PD reminded me that technological capability and educational value are not necessarily the same thing.

Just because an AI application can complete a task doesn't mean it is helping students learn.

That is something I want to keep questioning as I develop my own understanding.

I want to explore whether an AI tutor can offer hints, ask guiding questions and encourage students to attempt problems independently before receiving further support.

This connects directly to what I took away from Lauren's PD.

Looma: Student wellbeing and pastoral care

My experience as a boarding tutor has also inspired me to explore Looma, a student wellbeing application.

I'm interested in how AI and workflow automation could reduce repetitive administrative work, recognise positive student contributions and support progress tracking.

The idea also includes gamified digital companions that celebrate effort, improvement and achievement.

This project has made me think carefully about the responsibilities involved in developing AI systems, particularly when working with young people.

Privacy, safeguarding, fairness and human decision-making would need to be central to its design.

Year 11: Learning to build with AI

Another area I'm excited about is introducing practical AI development into the Digital Technologies curriculum.

I would love to develop a Year 11 unit where students learn how to connect applications to AI models using APIs, work with structured data and design their own AI-powered products or services.

My aim would be to move beyond teaching students how to prompt an AI tool.

I want them to understand enough about the technology to make informed design decisions, evaluate outputs and create something useful.

sections.title: What changed
sections.text:
I think the biggest change has been moving from understanding AI as a Computer Science concept towards exploring AI as something I can develop with.

Teaching AS91898 gave me valuable knowledge of how AI systems learn, operate and affect society.

My more recent exploration has introduced another layer: how to integrate these technologies into applications that respond to real needs.

I've also started looking at the upcoming changes to New Zealand's Digital Technologies and Computer Science curriculum with genuine excitement.

I see an opportunity to bring together theoretical understanding, programming, computational thinking and practical AI development.

I would love students to learn not only what machine learning or neural networks are, but also how AI services can become part of a larger software system.

At the same time, Lauren's PD reminded me that technological capability and educational value are not necessarily the same thing.

Just because an AI application can complete a task doesn't mean it is helping students learn.

That is something I want to keep questioning as I develop my own understanding.

sections.title: My reflection and next steps
sections.text:
What I've enjoyed most is being able to connect something I already know and teach with an entirely new area of learning.

I feel confident discussing the core concepts of AI because I have taught them, explored real-world examples and prepared students for external assessment.

But AI engineering is a different challenge, and I am still learning.

There are new tools, programming techniques, frameworks and design considerations to understand. I find myself researching, experimenting and occasionally getting things wrong.

I actually enjoy that part of the process.

It reminds me of my own teaching philosophy. I want my ākonga to be curious, to try difficult things and to see mistakes as part of learning. I need to be willing to do the same.

I believe we learn from one another. Even with my teaching experience and technical knowledge, there is still so much I can learn from other teachers, developers and the wider education community.

Looking ahead, I see several opportunities.

One is curriculum innovation, particularly as AI becomes more prominent in the Digital Technologies and Computer Science curriculum.

Another is developing and evaluating practical educational applications that could support students and teachers.

I am also interested in supporting colleagues through hands-on professional learning. Beyond introductory AI literacy and prompting, I would love to explore subject-specific applications, AI-supported workflows and opportunities for teachers to create useful tools for their own practice.

I don't see myself as someone who already knows everything about AI.

I see myself as a Computer Science teacher with a solid foundation, a genuine passion for technology and a willingness to keep learning.

My experience teaching AI gave me theoretical understanding. Lauren's PD encouraged me to think more critically about how AI should support learning. My independent exploration is helping me discover how I might turn these ideas into practical applications.

I want to keep learning, keep building and hopefully bring some of that excitement back into my classroom.

As I develop future AI learning activities, I want to make permitted AI use clear and check what students can explain and evaluate independently. Their own responses, including how they question reliability and bias, would help me judge whether the activity supports their thinking rather than simply produces a polished answer.

Date: Term 2 2026

This session made me reconsider something I do quite often: asking the class, "Does everyone understand?"

Usually a few students nod, and nobody says otherwise. I move on, assuming we're ready. But perhaps some ākonga are simply not comfortable admitting that they're confused.

The idea of using mini whiteboards to get a response from everyone really interested me.

I particularly liked that the PD explored using iPads as digital whiteboards through apps such as Freeform and Notability. Since our students already use iPads, this could be a practical way to check understanding without needing additional equipment.

In Computer Science, I can imagine asking everyone to predict the output of a short piece of pseudocode, identify an error, write a Boolean expression or explain what happens to a variable inside a loop.

Instead of hearing from the same confident students, I could see everyone's thinking at once.

The session also made me reflect on how I show care for students. I want students to feel safe making mistakes. If I use this strategy, it needs to feel like an opportunity to learn, not a way of catching someone out.

What I want to take forward: Try short, low-stakes questions using students' iPads, give them enough thinking time and use their responses to decide whether to move forward or revisit an explanation.

Date: Term 3 2026

I really connected with this session because it made me think about something I constantly balance in programming lessons: how much guidance should I give, and when should I step back?

I love project-based learning. I enjoy seeing ākonga experiment, solve problems and create something of their own.

But I also know what happens when students are given a task before they have enough understanding. Some become frustrated, while others rely heavily on the teacher or their classmates.

The Gradual Release of Responsibility model helped me think more deliberately about moving from teacher modelling to guided practice, collaboration and independent work.

The part that stayed with me was the importance of the middle stages.

Sometimes I explain a concept, demonstrate an example and then expect students to complete a task independently. I wonder whether I occasionally move too quickly from "I do" to "you do".

This is especially relevant when teaching new programming concepts. A student might follow my demonstration perfectly but still struggle to apply the same idea in a different situation.

I also appreciated that the model is flexible. Not every lesson needs to follow exactly the same sequence, and students with more experience may need less guidance.

What I want to take forward: Plan more opportunities for guided and collaborative practice before independent work, while continuing to give confident students the freedom to explore further.

Date: Term 3 2026

This session really made me think about the difference between understanding something today and remembering it several weeks later.

This is particularly relevant to Cambridge Computer Science, where students need to retain a large amount of theoretical knowledge and apply it in examinations.

I often feel pleased when students understand a concept during a lesson. But I have also experienced the frustration of revisiting the same topic later and discovering that much of it has been forgotten.

The idea of spaced retrieval made a lot of sense to me. Just because we've finished teaching a topic doesn't mean students have finished learning it.

I particularly liked the distinction between recognising information and actually being able to recall it without looking at notes.

It made me rethink revision. Instead of leaving most revision until the end of a unit, I want to bring older topics back regularly.

For example, a Cambridge Computer Science lesson on programming could begin with a few questions about data representation or hardware. A Python lesson could revisit loops, arrays or earlier concepts before introducing something new.

I also liked the idea of mixing questions from different topics so students need to decide which knowledge or method to use.

What I want to take forward: Develop a bank of short retrieval questions, revisit previously taught topics at planned intervals and encourage ākonga to see the effort of remembering as part of learning.

What I've enjoyed about this professional learning series is that the sessions connect with one another.

None of these ideas is completely unfamiliar to me. I already use quizzes, demonstrations, independent practice and revision activities. But the PD has encouraged me to think more carefully about why I use them and whether they are genuinely helping students learn.

I came from a design background and have always enjoyed creative, student-led projects. Sometimes I worry that too much structure might take away from that creativity.

What I'm beginning to appreciate is that explicit teaching and creativity don't need to compete. Giving students a strong foundation can actually make them more confident and independent when they begin creating.

I value learning from others, and I appreciate being part of a school where colleagues share their professional learning and challenge one another to think more deeply about teaching.

When I try iPad responses and spaced retrieval, I want to use students' answers to decide what to revisit and check their understanding again later. That would help me connect a calm, focused start with the explanations and practice each student needs, rather than judge a strategy by how busy the class looks.
